title: Buzzkill: How to defend Europe against drones – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Europe faces two linked drone threats — small drones disrupting airports and critical infrastructure, and Russian/Belarusian/Ukrainian military drones increasingly crossing into EU/NATO airspace at the eastern flank — with a stark cost asymmetry (Russia spends under €250,000 to force a European response costing millions); the EU's flagship Drone Defence Initiative is overly ambitious and likely to underdeliver, while national programs like Poland's €3.8bn anti-drone wall are the more credible near-term response the EU should fund and coordinate rather than replace.

insights.claim: Europe faces two distinct but related drone threats: small, civilian-flown drones disrupting airports and critical infrastructure with unclear attribution, and larger military drones crossing from Russia, Belarus and Ukraine into EU/NATO airspace at the eastern flank where the source is clear but intent is contested; the author argues technology and lessons should flow between the two rather than treating them as separate problems.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: The central organising thesis of the report: EU counter-drone investment should be designed for cross-application between military eastern-flank defense and civilian critical-infrastructure protection.

insights.claim: Every drone overflight or incursion, regardless of who is flying it, likely gives Russia intelligence on Europe's detection and interception capabilities, meaning the cumulative pattern of seemingly minor sightings has a compounding strategic reconnaissance value for Moscow.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Argues incident-by-incident dismissal of 'minor' drone sightings understates their cumulative strategic value to an adversary probing European defenses.
insights.quote: every time an overflight of critical infrastructure or incursion at the eastern flank happens, wherever it comes from, Russia learns something about Europe’s ability to fight (or otherwise) against these systems

insights.claim: Germany's aviation agency logged 227 drone sightings by pilots in 2025, a figure that has risen steadily since reporting began in 2020, with 2026 numbers on track to exceed it.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: A trackable, rising baseline metric for the scale of Europe's civilian drone-incursion problem.

insights.claim: On August 5 2026, a drone carrying explosive material was found and recovered at Leipzig airport in Germany; CCTV reportedly showed it flying toward a parked Antonov cargo plane, hitting a wing, and falling to the tarmac, where a bus driver discovered it — had the explosives detonated, the consequences could have been catastrophic, and this incident marks the first recovered armed drone at a European airport.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Marks an escalation from surveillance-only drone incidents to explosive-armed drones at civilian airports, raising the stakes for airport security investment.

insights.claim: Drone disruptions already carry measurable economic costs: Copenhagen airport closed for four hours in September 2025 after drone sightings, and more than 30 flights were cancelled in Munich following drone sightings in March 2025.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Quantifies near-term operational and revenue risk to European airports from drone disruptions, ahead of any conclusion on attribution.

insights.claim: In early 2025 Germany's defence ministry logged six drone overflights at Schwesing airbase, where Ukrainian soldiers train on Patriot air-defence systems; the drones may have carried signals-intelligence equipment to identify soldiers' mobile phones, potentially allowing Russia to later relocate those soldiers — and the scarce Patriot batteries with them — on the Ukrainian front line.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Illustrates a concrete drone-enabled SIGINT threat to Western military personnel and scarce equipment (Patriot batteries) even when drones fly over training sites far from the battlefield.

insights.claim: The drone threat sits within a broader documented Russian hybrid-sabotage campaign against Europe: igniting air-freight packages in Britain, Germany and Poland, damaging submarine cables in the Baltic Sea, a foiled plot (uncovered with US intelligence help) to assassinate Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger, and attacks on Sweden's telecommunications network.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Contextualises drone incidents as one arm of a wider, multi-vector Russian hybrid-warfare campaign against European infrastructure and defense-industry leadership.

insights.claim: A June 2026 report from the International Institute for Strategic Studies assessed it 'highly likely' that Russia conducted a drone campaign against Europe largely toward the end of 2025, with some drones traced back to Russian shadow-fleet vessels in the North and Baltic Seas.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: An independent assessment corroborating Russian state responsibility for the 2025 European drone campaign, strengthening the case for treating it as state-directed hybrid warfare.

themes.theme: Military incursions at the eastern flank

insights.claim: In September 2025, around 20 Russian military drones crossed into Polish airspace — the most serious incursion to date — prompting Poland to invoke Article 4 of NATO's Washington Treaty and triggering NATO's Operation Eastern Sentry.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: The defining escalation event that reframed drone incursions as a NATO Article 4-level security issue rather than a routine border nuisance.

insights.claim: Romania has become the most incident-prone eastern-flank state by mid-2026: it shot down three suspected Russian drones in three days in late July, and had recorded more than 40 airspace incursions in 2026 alone by the time of a June UN Security Council emergency session on the topic, a figure that continued growing afterward.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Identifies Romania as the current highest-frequency incursion hotspot, a leading indicator for where EU counter-drone funding urgency should concentrate.

insights.claim: In May 2026 a drone crashed into a ten-storey residential building in Galati, Romania, injuring a 14-year-old and his mother and forcing 70 evacuations; Romanian F-16s tracked the drone but could not fire on it due to 'operational reasons and certain legal limitations' — illustrating that legal and rules-of-engagement gaps, not just hardware, are blocking effective interception over populated areas during peacetime.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Shows that legal/regulatory clarity is as urgent a bottleneck as sensor or interceptor procurement for eastern-flank states.
insights.quote: operational reasons and [because of] certain legal limitations

insights.claim: Political accountability for drone-incursion response failures is already materialising: both Latvia's defence minister and prime minister lost their jobs over a perceived inadequate response to drone incursions, following a May 2026 incident that forced people to shelter in Vilnius, Lithuania.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Demonstrates real domestic political risk for eastern-flank governments perceived as under-responding to drone incidents.

insights.claim: In the September 2025 Polish incursion, NATO fighter jets (Polish F-16s and Dutch F-35s) shot down only three of roughly 20 incoming Russian Gerbera drones (an unarmed variant of the Iranian Shahed-136, costing around €10,000 each) using missiles costing several hundred thousand to a million euros apiece — meaning Russia likely spent under €250,000 to provoke a European response costing millions of euros, a stark and repeatable cost-exchange imbalance.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: The core economic argument for prioritising cheap kinetic and electronic-warfare counter-drone systems over fighter-jet interception — a clear opportunity signal for counter-drone startups versus reliance on legacy air-defense primes.
insights.quote: a single, only partly successful, counter-drone operation cost European countries millions, while Russia likely forked out less than €250,000 to prompt that response
insights.locator: Gerans and Gerberas / Drones crossing the eastern flank

insights.claim: Russia's Geran-3 drone (its own Shahed-136 derivative) can fly up to 800km, and Russia has used almost 1,000 drones in single-night attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure since 2025 — illustrating the scale of drone attack Europe could face if targeted with even a fraction of Ukraine's current exposure.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Provides a scale benchmark showing current European counter-drone capacity would be overwhelmed by even a fraction of Russia's demonstrated drone-attack volume against Ukraine.

insights.claim: Effective counter-drone defence requires a multi-layered 'system of systems': a detector layer (radar, electro-optical sensors, radio-frequency scanning, acoustic sensors), a defensive layer (electronic countermeasures, radio-frequency cyber-takeover, kinetic interceptors), and a command-and-control layer feeding a shared common operating picture — because no single sensor or effector type works reliably across all environments (forests, urban areas, agricultural land).
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: A technical procurement framework for evaluating any national or EU counter-drone program's completeness.
insights.locator: What a protected eastern flank looks like

insights.claim: Electronic countermeasures like GPS spoofing and RF jamming are already being defeated by battlefield adaptations seen in Ukraine — drones now carry up to 40km of fibre-optic cable to bypass jamming, and Ukraine's entire front line is now GPS-denied — showing counter-drone technology is in a fast-moving offense-defense arms race that any European procurement decision must account for as a moving target, not a static solution.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Warns against locking into a single counter-drone technology, since adversary countermeasures are evolving in near-real-time on the Ukrainian battlefield.

insights.claim: The EU's flagship 'European Drone Defence Initiative' (rebranded from 'drone wall') and 'Eastern Flank Watch' programmes are overly ambitious and risk failure: their stated scope covers border protection, migration, critical infrastructure, the southern flank and countering the Russian shadow fleet all under one 'dual-use' umbrella, a scope the author argues was likely inflated specifically to win funding buy-in from western European member states uninterested in eastern-flank-specific defense spending.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Suggests EU-level 'drone wall' funding announcements are more political messaging than executable near-term capability — investors and contractors should track scaled-down national programs as the more credible opportunity.
insights.quote: Such an all-encompassing proposal appears set for failure, however, and likely only became so inflated in the first place to placate member states away from the eastern flank.

insights.claim: National-level counter-drone efforts, not EU or NATO-wide programmes, currently look the most promising and advanced; the author argues the EU's role should be to fund and coordinate these national efforts (including via the SAFE defence-loan programme) rather than attempt to build a single unified pan-European system.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: A core policy recommendation: EU funding should flow to and coordinate national champions rather than compete with them via a separate centralized program.

themes.theme: Poland's anti-drone wall — the flagship national program

insights.claim: Poland's 'anti-drone wall,' reportedly Europe's largest counter-drone system, is budgeted at €3.8bn and being delivered by a consortium of the state-owned Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa, Norway's Kongsberg, and Poland's Advanced Protection Systems, with initial operational capability targeted by end of 2026 and full capability by end of 2027.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: A concrete, funded near-term revenue opportunity for Kongsberg and Polish defense primes, and a €3.8bn benchmark contract size for comparable eastern-flank national programs.

insights.claim: Poland's system specification includes 18 anti-drone batteries, 52 firing platoons, 18 command platoons and 703 military trucks and reconnaissance vehicles, with a defensive layer built on Kongsberg's 'Protector' weapon family — 35mm anti-aircraft guns, 30mm cannons, 12.7mm multi-barrel machine guns, laser-guided rockets and interceptor drones — plus electronic-warfare capability, and the drone wall is described as only one element of Poland's broader border fortification with Belarus and Kaliningrad.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Details the specific hardware mix (Kongsberg Protector systems) that could serve as a procurement template for other eastern-flank states.

themes.theme: Uneven eastern-flank readiness and the path forward

insights.claim: Baltic and Nordic counter-drone efforts lag Poland: the Estonian-led 'Baltic drone wall' consortium (including Polish and Finnish firms) had an EU funding request rejected in March 2025 and has yet to deliver a comprehensive system, though Estonia began deploying fixed drone-detection sensors along its Russian border in June 2026, and Finland allocated €44m in April 2026 for Border Guard drone detection and countermeasure procurement.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Identifies which eastern-flank programs (Baltic) are behind schedule despite active EU coordination discussions, and which national budgets (Finland's €44m) are now committed.

insights.claim: Bulgaria, Hungary and Slovakia remain the laggards on counter-drone defence: Hungary and Slovakia were initially absent from EU eastern-flank drone discussions, and Bulgaria has not yet made drone defences a priority despite facing the same threat exposure — leaving significant gaps in any future eastern-flank common operating picture.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Flags specific eastern-flank states where EU funding and diplomatic pressure would have the highest marginal impact on closing coverage gaps.

insights.claim: The author's five-point roadmap for the EU: (1) fund and accelerate advanced national efforts like Poland's and the Baltic states'; (2) fund laggards (Bulgaria, Hungary, Slovakia, Romania); (3) coordinate legal and regulatory best-practice sharing, citing Germany's reworked law letting its armed forces intercept drones and France's law letting private firms protect civilian infrastructure; (4) establish common NATO-aligned standards and certification for interoperability; (5) build a joint command-and-control node for a shared operating picture spanning the whole eastern flank from Finland to Bulgaria.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: A concrete, ranked EU policy agenda that could shape upcoming defense-budget allocation and legal-harmonisation debates.
insights.locator: How to turn the hotch-potch into a whole

insights.claim: Legal ambiguity is a live operational bottleneck, not just a hardware gap: a Romanian military representative noted a drone entering Romanian airspace in May 2026 was not intercepted partly because 'Ukraine is at war, but Romania is at peace,' leaving unclear legal authority to shoot down drones over a civilian setting in peacetime — a situation shared by all eastern-flank states.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Legal-framework harmonisation across the eastern flank is as urgent as sensor/interceptor procurement — a policy lever separate from defense spending.
insights.quote: Ukraine is at war, but Romania is at peace
insights.locator: How to turn the hotch-potch into a whole

insights.claim: The author explicitly warns that no amount of drone-defence buildup substitutes for ending the underlying Russian aggression against Ukraine and Russia's hybrid war against Europe; better defences only provide 'deterrence by denial' in the meantime, not a resolution to the threat.
insights.speaker: Ulrike Franke
insights.so_what: Frames all counter-drone capex as a stopgap deterrent, not a substitute for diplomatic/political resolution of the Russia-Ukraine war — a caveat on how far defense spending alone can solve the problem.
insights.quote: no build-up of European defences can replace diplomatic, political and military efforts to end the Russian aggression against Ukraine and Russia’s hybrid attacks against European nations
